newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Producers warned against betting on gold demand.
newsitem.headline: Producers warned against betting on gold demand.

text.p: Producers say physical demand for gold remains strong and that the bullion price will recover, but analysts warn against reading too much into a perceived gap between supply and demand.
Producers too often seemed to believe gold, once sold, vanished from the market, creating a vacuum between supply and demand that mines could fill with new production, analysts said.

"The market is always in equilibrium but it depends at what price. To say there is a gap between supply and demand is misleading. Gold is never taken off the market forever," said a gold hedging specialist.

"The only gold that stays off the market forever is the jewellery that Westerners buy...The Far East, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent all buy for a rainy day and they do sell back onto the market."
According to Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS), last year's total world gold supply was 3,490 tonnes. Analysts say that demand figures are misleading and inadequate.
"We've been accepting fabrication and demand figures far too much at face value. The demand side is odd and you can't tell where it's going. We don't have reliable numbers," said an analyst.
Total fabrication demand -- jewellery, electronics, official coins -- last year was 3,290 tonnes, according to GFMS.
Regional issues should be given more attention as countries, however underdeveloped or small, tend to shed gold reserves when money is needed, analysts said.

"We need to look at regional issues and crises because, while they often balance each other out (as far as gold sales or purchases go), sometimes they throw the market into disarray. Gold can come back (onto the market) when there is a local situation. I'm watching Cambodia very carefully at the moment," said one mining analyst.
The Cambodian capital Phnom Penh was hit by two days of fighting and a day of widespread looting and violence as forces loyal to the rival premiers battled for power.
World bullion price slid to 12-year lows late last Thursday on news that the Australian central bank had sold 167 tonnes of their gold reserves onto the market over the past six months.
Producers blame the actual announcement of the sales rather than the extra supply for moving the market and they say that physical demand for gold remains robust.
"We're going through a lot of pain right now but we need to look long-term," said Keith Spencer, general manager of Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd's GMFJ gold operations.
"There is a lot of negative sentiment about the Australian sales but the fall was triggered by the announcement. The market actually absorbed the gold sales," he added.
Spencer said physical demand for gold at the moment was the highest it had ever been.
